newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Dow seen volatile amid thin support.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Dow seen volatile amid thin support.

text.p: The lack of technical support under U.S. blue chips could lead to further volatility down the road, technical analysts said on Thursday.

After racing to a record high of 7333.55 on March 15, the Dow industrials and other major averages appear to be consolidating, with volume and volatility easing ahead of Monday's Memorial Day holiday.
The Dow was off about 33 points at 7258 in afternoon trading.

But the month-long 700-point decline that bottomed on April 11 at 6391.69 on the Dow, and the subsequent month-long runup that added about 950 points has been so sharp as to leave little in the way of a near-term base for the blue-chip average, technicians said.

"If the market does turn down sometime over the next few weeks or months, we're going to be hard-pressed to really define where we have support," said Ricky Harrington, technical analyst at Interstate/Johnson Lane.

Analysts noted that, in a bull market, pullbacks are typically limited to one-half of the most recent runup. This could give the Dow support at its "retracement level" between 6800 and 6900, they said.
The most solid support level could be back at the April low, they said.

"If you want to see actual support, you don't have it until the April low where we bounced," said Jonathan Dodd, technical analyst at Dean Witter. "But I doubt we're going to pull back to that level."
He cited strong momentum in stocks as providing an underpinning that could lead to an upside breakout in two-to-four weeks.
"If you get into June and we don't pull back more than half (of the recent upturn), than I think we're set up to run again," Dodd said.
Stocks will run into trouble, however, if the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond breaks out of the 6.75 to 7.00 percent trading range it has seen recently and drives above the 7.10 level, he said.
The long bond was off 11/32 to yield 6.99 percent on Thursday afternoon.
Harrington said "the best thing" for U.S. stocks would be an extended period of consolidation, with a slowdown in the high volume and the sharp moves that have characterized trading in recent weeks.
"But I don't that's going to be the case," he said. "It may abate for a day or two but I think that looking out over the next few weeks you're going to continue to see this volatility," he said.
